modules.title: Investor taxation
modules.subtitle: How your investments are taxed, how to pay only what's fair and which mistakes cost you dearly, with Spain as a detailed case study.
essentials: You're only taxed when you realise a gain (by selling) or receive income such as dividends and interest.
Well-managed losses reduce the tax you pay on your gains.
Time and the right vehicles (funds, pension plans, tax-advantaged accounts) make a big difference to the end result.

blocks.h: The basic principle: tax on realisation
blocks.html: While you don't sell, a rise is an unrealised gain and isn't taxed. When you sell, the difference between the sale price and the purchase price (after fees) is a capital gain or loss. Dividends and interest, on the other hand, are taxed in the year you receive them.

items.p: The difference between what you get when you sell and what it cost you, including buying and selling fees.
They're added to your savings income in the year you receive them. In Spain, 19% is already withheld at source.
It may be taxed at source and in your country. Tax treaties prevent double taxation, but sometimes you have to claim it back.

blocks.html: You sell for €18,000 some shares you bought for €10,000: a gain of €8,000. You pay 19% on the first €6,000 (€1,140) and 21% on the remaining €2,000 (€420). That's €1,560 in total, an effective rate of 19.5%.

blocks.h: The rules that save the most money in Spain
items: Offsetting losses: losses on sales are deducted from gains in the same year. If losses remain, you can offset up to 25% of dividends and interest, and anything left over can be carried forward for the next 4 years.
Fund switches: moving from one investment fund to another isn't taxed; you only pay when you redeem. This doesn't apply to ETFs or shares.
The two-month rule: if you sell listed securities at a loss and buy back equivalent securities in the two months before or after, you can't offset that loss until you sell the ones you bought back.
FIFO: when you sell part of a position bought in several instalments, you're deemed to sell the oldest units first.
International double taxation: foreign tax withheld on dividends can be deducted in your tax return up to the treaty limit (usually 15%).

pros: Contributions reduce your general taxable income: up to €1,500 a year, rising to €10,000 with employer contributions.
The tax saving is greater the higher your marginal rate is today.
cons: When you withdraw, the whole amount is taxed as employment income, not just the gain.
The money is locked in until retirement or specific situations, although since 2025 contributions made more than 10 years earlier can be withdrawn.
Many plans have high fees: compare them before signing up.

blocks.html: Reporting obligations: if you hold more than €50,000 in securities, accounts or assets abroad (for example, with a foreign broker), you must file form 720, or form 721 for crypto-assets held outside Spain. It doesn't mean paying more, but forgetting can be expensive.

items: Accumulating versus distributing: an accumulating fund reinvests dividends without them being taxed, so it defers tax and makes the most of compounding.
Tax-loss harvesting: realising losses to offset gains, while respecting the two-month rule.
Deferring is winning: paying tax later is like an interest-free loan from the tax authority that keeps working for you.
Other countries: France has the PEA, the UK has the ISA and Germany has an annual allowance (the Sparer-Pauschbetrag) of €1,000 per person.

blocks.html: Tax rules change. This information is general and up to date as of 2026: always check it with the tax authority or a tax adviser.

quiz.q: When, in general, is a rise in the price of your shares taxed?
o: Every 31 December, even if you don't sell
When you sell and realise the gain
When the price rises by more than 10%
quiz.e: Until you sell, the gain is unrealised and isn't taxed.

quiz.q: In Spain, what rate applies to the first €6,000 of savings income?
quiz.e: The first band of savings income is taxed at 19%.

quiz.q: You sell with a gain of €8,000. Roughly how much tax do you pay in Spain?
For how many years can unused losses be carried forward in Spain?
quiz.e: Unused losses can be applied over the following 4 years.

quiz.q: What advantage do switches between investment funds have in Spain?
o: They aren't taxed until you redeem
They reduce the income tax on your salary
quiz.e: A switch defers the tax: you only pay when you redeem.

quiz.q: You sell at a loss and buy the same thing back the following month. What happens?
o: You can still offset the loss
You can't offset that loss until you sell what you bought back
quiz.e: That's the two-month rule: the loss is put on hold.

quiz.q: Why can an accumulating fund be more tax-efficient?
o: Because it reinvests dividends without being taxed until you sell
Because it guarantees a higher return
quiz.e: By not paying out dividends, it defers tax and lets all your capital grow.

quiz.q: When do you have to file form 720?
o: When you hold more than €50,000 in assets or securities abroad
When you open an account with a Spanish bank
quiz.e: It's an information return on assets and rights held abroad.

modules.title: Derivatives: options, futures and CFDs
modules.subtitle: What they are, how leverage works and why most retail investors lose money with them.
essentials: A derivative is a contract whose value depends on another asset: you don't buy the share, but a right or a bet on it.
Leverage multiplies gains and losses, and can wipe you out far faster than you think.
Used well, they help hedge risks; used to speculate, they're the quickest way to lose money.

items.p: The right, but not the obligation, to buy (call) or sell (put) an asset at a set price (the strike) until a given date. You pay a premium for that right.
The obligation to buy or sell an asset at an agreed price on a future date. They trade on regulated exchanges and are settled daily.
A contract with your broker for the difference in an asset's price. They don't trade on an official exchange: your counterparty is the broker itself.

html: With €1,000 and 5:1 leverage you control a €5,000 position. If the asset rises 10%, you make €500: 50% on your money.
If it falls 10%, you lose €500, half your capital. And with a 20% fall, you lose everything. Leverage doesn't change the asset: it changes how quickly you're wiped out if you're wrong.

blocks.h: Maximum leverage for retail clients in the EU (ESMA)
head: Asset
Maximum
rows: Non-major currencies, gold and major indices
Commodities (other than gold) and non-major indices

blocks.html: By law, EU brokers must state what percentage of their retail clients lose money with CFDs: it's the majority, usually between 60% and 85%. ESMA also requires positions to be closed when margin falls to 50% and prohibits you from losing more than your account balance.

blocks.h: Options: how you win and how you lose
html: You buy a call with a €100 strike and pay a €4 premium. If the share is worth €115 at expiry, you make 15 − 4 = €11 per share. If it's worth €95, the option is worthless and you lose the €4 premium: an option buyer never loses more than the premium.
Whoever sold you the option takes the opposite bet: they collect the premium, but if the price soars their loss can be huge. That's why selling uncovered options is a game for professionals.

items: Protective put: buying a put on a share you already own works as insurance against falls.
Covered call: selling calls on shares you own generates income in exchange for giving up some of the upside.
Currency hedge: locking in today the exchange rate for an investment in dollars.
Portfolio hedge with futures: temporarily reducing your stock market exposure without selling your positions.

pros: They let you hedge specific risks at a known cost: the premium.
They make strategies possible that can't be built with shares alone.
A little capital buys a lot of exposure.
cons: Leverage speeds up losses and psychological pressure.
Time works against the option buyer.
CFDs carry daily financing costs, and the broker is your counterparty.

blocks.h: For those who want to go further

items: Time value: an option's premium is the sum of its intrinsic value and its time value, which evaporates as expiry approaches.
Implied volatility: the more the asset is expected to move, the more expensive options become, both calls and puts.
The Greeks: delta (sensitivity to price), theta (to the passage of time), vega (to volatility) and gamma (how much delta changes).
Contango and backwardation: in commodity futures, rolling contracts can cost or add return. That's why some commodity ETFs drift away from the spot price.

quiz.q: What does buying a call option give you?
o: The right, but not the obligation, to buy at a set price
quiz.e: A call is a right to buy at an agreed price (the strike) until a given date.

quiz.q: With €1,000 and 5:1 leverage, the asset falls 10%. How much do you lose?
quiz.e: You control €5,000: 10% is €500, half your capital.

quiz.q: What is the maximum leverage in the EU for a retail client trading CFDs on individual shares?
quiz.e: ESMA caps CFDs on individual shares at 5:1.

quiz.q: What is the most an option buyer can lose?
quiz.e: If the option expires worthless, the buyer only loses the premium.

quiz.q: What is a protective put for?
o: As insurance against falls in a share you already own
quiz.e: The put gains value if the share falls, offsetting the loss.

quiz.q: Who is the counterparty in a CFD?
o: The company that issued the share
quiz.e: CFDs are contracted directly with the broker, not on a regulated exchange.

quiz.q: What happens to an option's time value as expiry approaches?
quiz.e: The less time left, the less the chance of the price moving in your favour is worth.

quiz.q: According to brokers' mandatory warnings, what share of retail clients lose money with CFDs?
quiz.e: The mandatory warnings show that most retail accounts lose money.

modules.title: Valuing companies: DCF and multiples
modules.subtitle: Estimate what a business is really worth and decide whether its share price makes sense.
essentials: A company is worth the cash it will generate in the future, brought back to today's value.
Multiples (P/E, EV/EBITDA) make quick comparisons possible; a DCF forces you to think about the business.
Every model depends on assumptions: always insist on a margin of safety.

blocks.html: A euro in ten years' time is worth less than a euro today, because today you could invest it. A discounted cash flow (DCF) estimates the free cash flow the company will generate each year and brings it back to present value with a discount rate that reflects the risk.

items: Free cash flow (FCF): the cash the business generates after investing to maintain itself and grow.
Projection: estimate how much that cash flow will grow over the next 5 to 10 years.
Terminal value: the value of all the years after that, assuming modest perpetual growth (2–3%).
Discounting: bring each cash flow back to today with the discount rate (for example, 8–10% for a mature company).
From company value to share value: subtract net debt and divide by the number of shares.

head: Item
Value
rows: Present value of the cash flows for years 1–5
Present value of the terminal value

blocks.html: Notice that three quarters of the value comes from the terminal value: small changes in the discount rate or in perpetual growth move the result a lot. That's why a DCF gives a range, not an exact figure. Try it in the DCF calculator among the Premium tools.

items.p: Price ÷ earnings per share. Simple, although accounting profit can be dressed up.
Enterprise value (including debt) ÷ operating profit before depreciation and amortisation. It lets you compare companies with different debt levels.
Price ÷ free cash flow. It measures how much you pay for the real cash the business generates.
Price ÷ book value. Useful for banks and insurers; less so for software companies.

blocks.html: If you estimate that a share is worth €34 and it trades at €25, you have a 26% margin of safety. Benjamin Graham, the father of value investing, advised buying only with a wide margin, because your estimates can be wrong.

items: Value traps: a company can be cheap because its business is in decline.
Optimistic growth: few companies grow by more than 10% a year for a decade.
Paying in shares: if a company pays its employees in shares, it dilutes shareholders even though no cash goes out.
Cyclical companies: their P/E looks lowest right at the top of the cycle, when profits are exceptional.
WACC: the weighted average of the cost of debt (after tax) and the cost of equity.
Cost of equity: usually estimated as the risk-free rate + beta × the market risk premium (the CAPM model).
Sensitivity: always calculate the value with several rates and growth figures. If the conclusion changes with a one-point difference, the investment isn't that clear.

quiz.q: What does a DCF estimate?
o: The price the share will trade at tomorrow
The present value of the cash the company will generate
quiz.e: A DCF adds up future cash flows brought back to today's value.

quiz.q: Why are future cash flows discounted?
o: Because a future euro is worth less than a euro today
quiz.e: Today's money can be invested, and the future is also uncertain.

quiz.q: In the example, what share of the value comes from the terminal value?
quiz.e: About 1,506 of 1,992 million: around 75%.

quiz.q: What advantage does EV/EBITDA have over P/E?
o: It takes debt into account and lets you compare companies with different debt levels
quiz.e: Enterprise value includes net debt, which P/E ignores.

quiz.q: According to your analysis, a share is worth €40 and trades at €30. What's your margin of safety?
What is a value trap?
o: A company that's cheap because its business is getting worse
quiz.e: It looks like a bargain, but the low price reflects real deterioration.

quiz.q: What perpetual growth rate is reasonable when calculating a terminal value?
quiz.e: In the very long run, no company grows much faster than the economy.

quiz.q: Why can the P/E of a cyclical company be misleading at the top of the cycle?
o: Because profits are exceptionally high, making the share look cheap
Because those companies have no P/E
quiz.e: With peak profits, the P/E looks low just before they fall.

modules.title: Advanced risk management and trading psychology
modules.subtitle: The maths that separates those who survive in the markets from those who are wiped out.
essentials: What matters isn't being right often, but winning more when you're right than you lose when you're wrong.
Large losses are disproportionately hard to recover from.
A journal and written rules protect your money from your emotions.

html: A system's expectancy is what you win or lose on average per trade: (win rate × average win) − (loss rate × average loss).
With 40% of trades winning €3 and 60% losing €1, expectancy is 0.4 × 3 − 0.6 × 1 = +€0.60 for every euro risked. You can be wrong more often than you're right and still make money.

blocks.html: That's why professionals obsess more about not losing much than about winning a lot. Protecting your capital is the first rule; growing it is the second.

items: Fixed fraction: always risk the same percentage of your capital (for example, 1%) on each trade. After a bad run, positions shrink automatically.
The Kelly criterion: optimal fraction = p − (1 − p) ÷ R, where p is the win rate and R the reward-to-risk ratio. With p = 0.4 and R = 3, Kelly suggests 20%.
Half Kelly: Kelly is very aggressive and your estimates are never exact, so many professionals use half or less.
Correlated risk: five positions in the same sector aren't five different risks, but one big one.

items.p: Increasing your size after a loss to win it back quickly. It's the fastest way to turn a bad day into a disaster.
Opening trades out of boredom or a need for action. Each one pays fees and the spread.
Pushing your stop-loss further away as the price approaches it. It turns a small, planned loss into a big one.
A good decision can turn out badly and a bad one can turn out well. Judge whether you followed the plan, not just whether you made money.

items: Before entering: note why you're entering, where your stop is, what your target is and how much you're risking.
While it's open: record any change to the plan and why.
On exit: note the result, how you felt and whether you kept to your rules.
Every month: calculate your win rate, your average win and loss and your real expectancy.

pros: They protect you during bad runs.
cons: No rule works in every market.
They demand discipline even when they hurt.
Too many rules can paralyse you.

items: Losing streaks: with a 50% win rate, a run of 6 or 7 losses in a row over 100 trades is normal. Your position size must be able to handle it.
Risk of ruin: the probability of losing so much capital that you can't recover. It grows very quickly as you increase the risk per trade.
Monte Carlo simulations: repeating a random sequence of trades with your statistics thousands of times shows the range of possible outcomes, not just the average. Try it in the Premium tools.

quiz.q: You're right 40% of the time with an average win of €3 and wrong 60% of the time with an average loss of €1. What's your expectancy per trade?
If you lose 50% of your capital, how much do you need to gain to get it back?
quiz.e: With half the money, you have to double it to get back to where you started.

quiz.q: What does fixed-fraction sizing involve?
o: Always risking the same percentage of capital per trade
Always buying the same number of shares
Doubling the bet after a loss
quiz.e: Risk adjusts automatically to the size of the account.

quiz.q: According to Kelly, with p = 0.5 and R = 2, what fraction of capital should you risk?
Why do many professionals use half Kelly?
o: Because Kelly is very aggressive and estimates are never exact
Because Kelly only works for options
quiz.e: Reducing size cuts volatility a lot in exchange for a little return.

quiz.q: What is revenge trading?
o: Increasing your size after a loss to win it back quickly
quiz.e: It's an emotional reaction that usually makes losses bigger.

quiz.q: Why is it dangerous to move your stop-loss further away as the price approaches it?
o: It turns a small, planned loss into a big one
quiz.e: The stop exists to cap the loss you accepted in advance.

quiz.q: With a 50% win rate, is a run of 6 losses in a row over 100 trades unusual?
o: Only if the system is bad
quiz.e: The longest expected losing streak is around 6 or 7 in a row.

montecarlo.p: Enter your statistics and see 100 possible paths for your account. Discover what the average doesn't tell you.
montecarlo.lossProb: Probability of ending with a loss
montecarlo.positive: Your system has positive expectancy: in the long run it tends to make money, although there will be tough streaks along the way.
montecarlo.negative: Your system has negative expectancy: the more trades you make, the more likely you are to lose.
montecarlo.note: Each simulation uses random, independent trades with your statistics. Fees and slippage are not included.

drawdown.p: Find out how much you need to gain to recover from a fall and how many years it could take.
drawdown.chartLabel: Gain needed depending on the fall
drawdown.explain: A fall of {loss} requires a rise of {need}. At {r} a year it would take about {n} years to get back to where you started.

fire.p: Work out the wealth you'd need to live off your investments and how long it would take to build it.
fire.expenses: Annual spending you want to cover
fire.chartLabel: Growth of your wealth towards the target
fire.progress: You already have {p} of the target.
fire.note: The 4% rule comes from historical US studies (the Trinity Study): withdrawing 4% in the first year and adjusting for inflation lasted 30 years in most scenarios. It isn't a guarantee; for longer horizons, many people use 3–3.5%.

dcf.p: Estimate a share's intrinsic value from its free cash flow and compare it with its price.
dcf.under: Based on your assumptions, the share trades below its estimated value.
dcf.over: Based on your assumptions, the share trades above its estimated value.
dcf.sensTitle: Sensitivity: value per share by discount rate (rows) and perpetual growth (columns)
dcf.errRate: The discount rate must be higher than perpetual growth.
dcf.note: A DCF is only as good as its assumptions. Use the sensitivity table to see a reasonable range, not an exact figure.
